transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-14 16:00 PST
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Patrick O'Rourke (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Jonah Park (AstroHealth CTO), Sara Kim (ML Eng), Luis Rivera (Infra), Meera Patel (PM)

Summary:
Quick discovery to gather latency and throughput targets for AstroHealth's conversational summarization service. Primary goals: p95 latency targets for short and long contexts, concurrency and streaming constraints, and whether Hosted, Dedicated, or Private deployment makes sense given security and performance. Discussed token/sec benchmarks, KV caching behavior, batching tradeoffs, and fallback policies.

Topics: p95 latency (short utterances ~32-64 tokens, long context ~2k tokens), concurrency targets (user-visible concurrency and background batching), streaming vs non-streaming, token/sec and tokens-per-second benchmarking, dedicated sizing for 8–16 concurrent sustained requests, expected 1k qps bursts on weekdays.

--- Transcript body (timestamps intermittent, auto-transcribed, imperfect) ---
[00:00] Patrick: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. I think we have about an hour, so we'll focus on the latency and throughput bits and then line up next steps. Maya's gonna cover the benchmarks side, I'll cover product/contract fit.
[00:12] Jonah: Thanks. To set expectations, we are evaluating three modes — your hosted API for fast integration, dedicated pools for steady throughput, and private VPC for regulatory stuff. Our hard constraint is p95 under 400ms for short replies and p95 under 2s for long context summaries, those are basically our SLOs.
[00:30] Maya: Okay, great. When you say short replies, is that ~16–64 tokens or are we looking micro-responses? Also, do you have streaming enabled in the UX?
[00:42] Sara: For chat quick responses it'd be 16–64 tokens yes, and we definitely use streaming for partial text as the user types — so latency to first token matters a lot. For end-of-chat summaries with 1.5–2k context it's less about streaming and more about total tail latency.
[00:58] Luis: One more infra note: our security team will push hard for VPC/private on PHI flows, but for non-PHI we can go hosted if latency/costs are okay.
[01:10] Patrick: Makes sense. Two quick data points from other customers - when streaming is used p95 to first token is often the key metric and sometimes it's 30–120ms on dedicated hardware depending on model size and quantization. On hosted we typically see higher variability because of multi-tenant scheduling.
[01:28] Maya: Right, and also the way we do continuous batching can affect that. If you have low concurrency we might hold micro-batches for a few ms to reach throughput targets. We can tune for latency-first or cost-first.
[01:40] Jonah: We need latency-first for short chat, cost-aware for bulk summarization jobs. Can you walk through what numbers you'd expect for p95 on hosted vs dedicated for, say, a 13B model at 1k context and at 2k context?
[01:55] Maya: Sure. Rough ballpark: 13B fp16 on dedicated GPU (A10/H100-ish) - for 1k context p95 generation until completion might be in the 400–800ms range for short outputs, whereas for 2k context it's commonly 800ms–1.8s depending on decode length. On hosted you'd add variability — maybe +20–40% and occasional spikes if there's cross-tenant contention. But if you enable streaming the first token p95 could be under 120–150ms on dedicated, and 150–300ms hosted.
[02:25] Sara: Those are helpful. What's the tokens/sec throughput you see on a single GPU for steady decodes? We have a lot of background batch summarization jobs during nights and need cost estimates.
[02:36] Maya: For autoregressive decodes tokens/sec depends on model size and quantization: 13B fp16 maybe 60–120 tokens/sec sustained on one A100-class GPU with optimized kernels; with 8-bit or 4-bit quantization and optimized runtime you can push higher—maybe up to 200–400 tokens/sec for some workloads. But that's a wide range. Our Optimize tool will suggest quant profiles per workload.
[02:58] Luis: Is that tokens/sec per core or per card? We use multi-card setups for Dedicated.
[03:04] Maya: Per GPU/card as configured for inference. With multi-gpu sharding parallelism is different; usually we keep a single model replica per GPU for low-latency serving. For huge throughput we use batching or shard across GPUs but that increases cross-GPU coordination overhead.
[03:22] Patrick: Quick interjection — for your concurrency matrix, if you expect 8–16 sustained convs with occasional 1k qps bursts, Dedicated with autoscaling + burst capacity is the usual fit. Hosted is fine for exploratory workloads but dedicated gives predictability for p95 SLOs.
[03:38] Jonah: We are trying to avoid big wastage. What's the typical instance sizing for 8 concurrent users with streaming requirements and a 13B model?
[03:47] Maya: If those 8 are interactive and need sub-200ms first-token, you might want 4–8 GPU replicas (depending on GPU class) configured with low batch windows. So it's less about vCPU and more about GPU hours; the math depends on expected request length and tokens/sec. We'll provide a sizing worksheet.
[04:06] Meera: Can you also talk about prefix/KV cache behavior? We pre-populate system prompts and long conversation state, and cache hit ratio is important to us.
[04:14] Maya: Our runtime supports KV caching for transformer models — that reduces compute for repeated context significantly. If you keep long histories in the cache, subsequent tokens only require the decode portion. The tricky bit for hosting is cache warm-up on cold starts and multi-tenant eviction policies. Dedicated or Private lets you control eviction and warm-starts.
[04:32] Sara: Do you have metrics on p95 with warm KV cache vs cold?
[04:36] Maya: We've seen p95 drop by 30–70% on decode for many sequences when a KV cache is fully warmed — e.g., long context completions that would be 1.5s cold can go down to 400–700ms warm. But depends on the ratio of prompt vs generated tokens.
[04:53] Jonah: Got it. Luis, will your infra team be able to run a flywheel with our data?
[04:58] Luis: We'll need a test plan and some scripts. We prefer Redwood to drive the initial baseline — run hosted and dedicated runs with our sample corpus then we can reproduce on-prem later. Also need KMS/HSM integration notes for Private.
[05:13] Patrick: We'll own the hosted baseline and propose a dedicated run plan — will include token/sec, latency histograms, and concurrency scenarios. We'll share a spreadsheet for you to fill out your prompt distribution.
[05:25] Sara: About streaming, can we buffer partial tokens or use delta updates? Our frontend expects chunked deltas about every 100–200ms.
[05:33] Maya: Yes, Redwood streaming supports chunked chunks — we try not to buffer more than a few tens of ms if latency-first. For delta updates the frontend can request partial outputs; our SDKs support that. There is tradeoff if you enable aggressive batching we buffer more.
[05:48] Jonah: We also flagged p99 for compliance — if p99 spikes above X we need retries and fallback to a smaller model. How does Redwood handle graceful degradation?
[05:58] Maya: We have policy routing and automatic fallback — you can configure a cheaper/smaller model or a lower-quality decode path if latency spikes or if the designated pool is saturated. We also do region failover. Note: fallbacks mean different generation quality, so you should have a product-level acceptance test.
[06:18] Meera: Related to tokenization — our workloads have lots of medical terms; tokenization variability affects tokens/sec. Does Redwood provide per-prompt tokenization stats during benchmarks?
[06:27] Maya: We do. We'll run analysis showing tokenization delta vs plain english baseline and include it in the benchmark sheet.
[06:33] Jonah: Okay let's dig into a concrete test. We'll give you 10k sample queries spanning short chat and long summary, and we want a hosted baseline and a dedicated run. For dedicated run: measure p50/p90/p95/p99 latency to first token and completion, and tokens/sec sustained for long decodes. Schedule and timelines?
[06:47] Patrick: Proposed timeline: you drop the corpus by 2025-02-18. We'll run hosted quick test same week and share initial numbers. Then set up a 2–3 day dedicated benchmark (week of 2/24) with Maya running the dedicated runs.
[06:58] Sara: Sounds good. For dedicated runs do you simulate traffic (concurrency matrix) or run single-client sequential? We need both.
[07:05] Maya: We'll do both: synthetic concurrency tests to reproduce p95 and then a replay of your real traffic to measure end-to-end. We'll include streaming-first-token metrics.
[07:14] Jonah: How do you handle warm caches during those runs? We want warm and cold numbers.
[07:19] Maya: We'll do controlled cold starts (flush cache) and then warm runs after preloading conversations. We'll document warm-up time.
[07:27] Luis: Another infra question: we run in Azure, any constraints with certain instance types?
[07:33] Maya: Dedicated can run on your cloud of choice via our dedicated pools — we support major cloud providers. For Private/On-prem we provide an installer and images; there are some kernel and driver requirements and you'll need GPU drivers, CUDA, and a supported NCCL. We'll share a compatibility matrix.
[07:48] Patrick: Quick practical: for your 1k qps burst piece — is that user-visible or internal batch jobs?
[07:55] Jonah: That's external — webhooks from many users at peak times. Typical sustained 800–1200 qps for 20–30 seconds, with an average request size of ~40 tokens and some longer ones.
[08:05] Maya: For spiky workloads we recommend a mix: Dedicated baseline sized for sustainable usage plus burst capacity to handle short spikes — or use hosted for burst traffic while routing sensitive PHI to dedicated/private pools.
[08:18] Sara: Any specific guidance on batching strategy for mixed workloads? We need to balance tail latency for interactive and throughput for nightly jobs.
[08:26] Maya: The main knobs are batch window (ms), max batch size, and whether you allow cross-request batching across tenants. For your setup we'd recommend a small batch window (5–20ms) for interactive routes and larger batch windows for background jobs. Also, prefix caching heavily reduces cost for repeated contexts.
[08:40] Patrick: I'll add this: Redwood Optimize will run heuristics on your historical traffic (once you opt-in) and suggest per-route batch/window configs.
[08:49] Jonah: About monitoring and tracing — we need token-level latency breakdowns and the ability to tie slow requests to prompts.
[08:56] Maya: Console provides token-level cost & latency breakdown, and you can attach trace ids to requests. We'll show a sample trace in the demo.
[09:05] Luis: Security note again: our security lead will require KMS with customer-managed keys, and audit logs for model versions and prompt access. How mature are those features?
[09:15] Patrick: We support KMS integrations, audit logs in Console, and role-based access controls. For Private deployments you can have the control plane in your VPC and bring your own KMS/HSM. We'll share SOC2 and technical security whitepaper.
[09:28] Sara: For the dedicated PoC, can we run a smaller model fallback that has identical tokenization but lower latency so we can compare quality/latency tradeoffs?
[09:36] Maya: Yes, part of the PoC we'll run a 7B variant as a fallback model and run A/B quality against the 13B. We'll include automated evals on your prompt set.
[09:44] Jonah: Any potential gotchas with streaming + KV cache? For example, if we stream partial outputs while also relying on KV cache for prior tokens…
[09:52] Maya: Streaming and KV cache interplay is mostly fine. The cache is for autoregressive past key values — streaming sends decoded tokens as they are produced. If you pre-warm cache and then stream decodes, you get the low-latency first token and reduced compute for subsequent tokens. The main gotcha is if you shard across GPUs you might need to coordinate cache placements.
[10:08] Meera: On metrics, could you provide example histograms and a CSV of p50/p90/p95/p99 across deciles?
[10:16] Patrick: Yes, benchmark artifact will include histograms, tokenization deltas, and a csv. We'll share a link to a sample benchmark deck (link).
[10:23] Patrick: I'll drop a note — doc: https://redwood-internal.example/benchmarks/astrohealth (demo link, access perms will be set)
[10:30] Sara: Regarding cost estimates — do you provide per-token cost under different quantization and batching profiles?
[10:37] Maya: Yep, Redwood Optimize will estimate unit token cost factoring in batch sizes, cache hit ratios, and quantization. We'll produce a cost model for hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[10:45] Jonah: For our compliance folks, what about data retention and ability to disable retention?
[10:49] Patrick: Hosted defaults to ephemeral logs for inference but enterprise contracts can opt-out of telemetry or configure retention. In Dedicated and Private you can control logs and retention. We'll include that in the security packet.
[11:00] Luis: One more engineering ask: provide the exact graph of latency vs concurrency for a 13B model on your recommended GPU. We need to test capacity planning.
[11:09] Maya: We'll produce that in the dedicated run. It will show p50/p95 latency curves over concurrency sweep.
[11:16] Jonah: Ok let's recap next steps.
[11:18] Patrick: Recap: 1) AstroHealth provides 10k sample queries + concurrency matrix by 2025-02-18. 2) Redwood runs quick hosted baseline same week and shares sheet. 3) Redwood schedules dedicated baseline week of 2025-02-24 — Maya runs tests and shares artifacts. 4) Share SOC2/KMS/security docs to Luis. 5) Follow-up call to review results and sizing. Anything to add?
[11:45] Meera: Can we also get a short cost estimate for 3-month Dedicated reserve vs pay-as-you-go hosted for our projected usage?
[11:50] Patrick: Yes we'll include that in the pricing note.
[11:53] Jonah: Great, thanks.
[11:55] Patrick: Thanks everyone — we'll send the sheet and schedule the dedicated run.
[11:59] Meeting end.
